results.title: Port 80: What It Is Used For and How It Works | SSHFlow
results.snippet:
Port 80 is the conventional default for HTTP, usually carried over TCP in ordinary web browsing. HTTP on this port is not encrypted by itself, while HTTPS conventionally uses port 443 and TLS. A website may keep port 80 available for HTTPS redirects or HTTP-based certificate validation. To assess an open port, identify the listening service and check the relevant firewall and network path; the port number alone does not tell you whether the service is vulnerable or reachable from outside. [...] Port 80 is the conventional default port for HTTP, the protocol traditionally used to load websites without transport encryption. When you visit an address such as ` without specifying a port, a browser normally connects to the server on TCP port 80. Port 80 is a network endpoint number, not the HTTP protocol or a guarantee about which application is listening there.

Quick answer [...] In everyday web use, HTTP on port 80 normally runs over TCP. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TCP connections. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP and is generally associated with HTTPS on port 443; it is not the usual meaning when someone asks whether port 80 is TCP or UDP.

The GUI and SCI protocols use default ports that can be modified using the configuration wizard.

The GUI can use both HTTP and HTTPS. The SCI protocol uses only HTTPS to secure for the credentials passed in each request. By default, these two protocols are on their standard port number of 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS. You can modify these ports in the GUI (see Launch the Configuration Wizard).
